## Proposed components and interactions

1. A Python 3.12 Flask **application factory** injects an in-memory `MemoryStore`, a UTC-aware `Clock` (`now()`), a cryptographic token generator, and a private `MemoryNotificationSink`. The factory seeds only synthetic identities with password **hashes**, configures a local secret key through a documented non-production mechanism, and registers server-rendered templates/routes. A new factory instance per pytest case isolates test state. No external identity, mail, database, JS application, or deploy integration.
2. **Identity/session service:** normalize the submitted email consistently (trim and case-fold for the synthetic account index), verify stored password hashes with a standard password-hashing API, issue an unpredictable server-side session identifier, and store its digest, account ID and account `session_epoch` in `MemoryStore`. Flask's signed, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie carries only the opaque session identifier and CSRF secret, not proof of authorization by itself. Each protected request must look up the identifier in the registry **and** compare its epoch with the current account epoch. Sign-in creates a fresh identifier; sign-out removes it and clears the cookie. A successful reset increments the epoch and removes that account's registry entries. Previously issued cookies in *every* client then fail the next protected request even though the browser still has a signed cookie. No reliance on clearing only the browser that submitted the reset.
3. **Recovery service:** handle syntactically valid email submissions, apply a per-*known*-account rolling 3600-second acceptance window, issue a cryptographically random URL-safe bearer token on each of the first five accepted requests, store only `SHA-256(token)` keyed reset records with account ID, UTC `issued_at` and consumed state, and deliver the full locally constructed reset link only into the **private** in-memory sink. The sixth request in-window creates no token/link; at the window boundary the oldest accepted request ages out. Unknown emails create no account record, token or notification. All otherwise equivalent syntactically valid POSTs, including known/unknown/throttled, render the same status, response headers and server-rendered acknowledgement body without identifier, quota or link; avoid account-dependent redirects, flashes and cookies. This is observable response parity, not a demonstrated constant-time guarantee; timing and multi-process abuse resistance remain production limitations.
4. **Reset service:** validate the bearer token digest both on display and, decisively, within a store lock on POST. The usable interval is `now < issued_at + 30 minutes` and token is not consumed; at the exact boundary it is invalid. On a validated new-password POST, prepare the new password hash and notification event, then under the **same lock** recheck token and expiry and atomically publish a replacement in-memory state snapshot comprising password hash update, consumed token, incremented session epoch, removal of that account's active sessions, and **one owner-addressed notification event**. The snapshot/commit boundary prevents two concurrent successful submissions or a public success before the notification is recorded; only a committed reset gets the success response. A replay, malformed token, expired token, CSRF failure or invalid input does not change account/password/session state or append a success notification. Retain consumed token digests while their original expiry is relevant; garbage-collect expired records without making them usable again.
5. **Server-rendered UI:** one shared local stylesheet and semantic HTML templates; no external assets. Use the observed sign-in composition literally. The *proposed*, unpictured reset-request page has a labeled email input and submit button, identical generic acknowledgement on successful-format submissions, and return-to-sign-in link. The *proposed*, unpictured new-password page has a labeled `type=password` field and neutral invalid/used/expired-link page with a fresh-request link; success shows a neutral sign-in link. The authenticated result is a minimal `/account` page solely to demonstrate session validity. Labels use `for`/`id`, focus is visible, error text is associated with the relevant field, and all controls are keyboard operable. These are implementation choices, not image observations.

### HTTP and in-process contracts (proposed)

| Interface | Input and behavior | Public result / private effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /sign-in` | Render sign-in form, generate anonymous CSRF secret if absent. | `200` HTML with pictured card. |
| `POST /sign-in` | Email, password and CSRF token; compare synthetic account password hash. | On success rotate session ID and go to `/account`; otherwise generic form error, no password echo. A CSRF failure cannot sign in. |
| `GET /account`; `POST /sign-out` | Read cookie session ID; guard looks up registry and matching epoch on **every** protected request. Sign-out requires CSRF. | Active sessions receive minimal account page; stale/revoked cookies are rejected/redirected to sign-in and cleared. |
| `GET /forgot-password` | Link target from sign-in. | `200` HTML labeled email request form. |
| `POST /forgot-password` | Email and CSRF; for syntactically valid identifiers use recovery service. | Identical `200` acknowledgement for known, unknown and known-but-throttled identifiers; only an eligible known account emits a link to private sink. Invalid syntax/CSRF gets field-specific feedback, independent of account existence. |
| `GET /reset/<token>` | Decode URL-safe bearer token, digest for lookup, check unused/unexpired. | Valid: `200` server-rendered new-password form. Otherwise one neutral unavailable-link response with fresh-request route; no account/token details. |
| `POST /reset/<token>` | CSRF and nonempty new password; revalidate and consume within one locked operation. | One successful update + revoked sessions + one owner notification then neutral success; invalid/used/expired token returns neutral unavailable-link response. No password or token in success content. |
| `MemoryNotificationSink` | Internal `record_link(account_id, url, issued_at)` and `record_success(account_id, occurred_at)` / read-only snapshot in test fixture or same-process local REPL. | No HTTP route, public page, debug endpoint, log dump or external email exposes sink data. Links are bearer secrets, accessible only to explicitly authorized local tests/demonstration code. Notification event addresses the synthetic account owner without including a password or reset token. |

The form CSRF contract is a per-client random secret stored in Flask's signed cookie and a matching hidden form token, checked on **all POSTs**; signing prevents client modification but is not encryption. Configure cookie `Secure` for HTTPS deployment (the localhost HTTP demonstration cannot claim HTTPS), `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, and restrict methods to those listed. Render with Jinja autoescaping, use parameterized internal route generation and no external resources, add `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on pages carrying reset tokens, and avoid tokens/passwords in logs, exceptions and analytics. A GET never consumes a token. Server should not trust referer as CSRF defense. Unauthenticated acknowledgement must not expose whether a link was issued.

### State, time and operational boundaries

`MemoryStore` owns `accounts[email] = {id, password_hash, session_epoch}`, `sessions[digest(session_id)] = {account_id, epoch}`, `reset_requests[account_id] = [accepted_issued_at...]`, `tokens[digest(token)] = {account_id, issued_at, consumed}`, plus the private sink's link/success event lists. A single process-wide lock coordinates accepted-request counting and token issuance (prevent racing sixth requests), as well as atomic reset completion and concurrent session creation: sign-in must read current password and epoch and insert its session under the same synchronization boundary used by reset, so a stale credential cannot install a valid pre-reset session after completion. Expired request timestamps are pruned with `timestamp <= now - 3600s`; reset-token expiry is computed from **issuance** rather than first visit or form submission. `Clock` is injected into all state transitions and tests, with fixed UTC-aware instants and boundary advances; no sleeps. Token generator uses OS cryptographic randomness in the app; a deterministic source may be injected only by tests. Tests use multiple independent Flask clients with distinct cookie jars to prove all-session invalidation and race/replay behavior.

Nothing survives a process restart, and state is neither shared nor safe across multiple workers. No schema migration exists for this local demonstration; production would require transactional durable account/token/session/rate-limit data, managed secret rotation, reliable notification delivery/outbox, centralized auditing/monitoring and multi-instance synchronization. Do not present the local sink as an email service or claim that successful appends prove external delivery. Privacy-conscious local observability may count **accepted/suppressed/consumed/revoked** events without user IDs, links or password values in public logs; pytest asserts the private sink. Never deploy or add a deployment workflow/instructions.

## Significant design decisions and alternatives

| Decision | Alternatives considered | Reason / qualification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python 3.12 Flask factory + Jinja server rendering and pytest | SPA/API, persistent service | Matches story REQ-018/019/022, isolates state/time in tests; no app exists yet. |
| Synthetic account hashes and process-local store/sink | Real user directory, DB, SMTP | Fits story REQ-020/021 and local demonstration; does not satisfy production durability or delivery. |
| Server registry plus account epoch for cookie sessions | Flask signed client session as sole authentication authority, or clearing only resetter's cookie | Both alternatives leave other previously issued cookies valid; per-request epoch check revokes all. |
| Digest-only reset token index; raw URL confined to sink | Store plaintext tokens in index, put reset link in public acknowledgement | Limits token exposure and avoids account disclosure; private sink still contains sensitive link intentionally for local inspection. |
| Rolling known-account issuance quota | Fixed hourly bucket or inferred unknown-account quota | A rolling 3600-second window prevents bucket-boundary bursts; standard specifies per account, not a quota for nonexistent identities. Response parity holds regardless. |
| Revalidate and snapshot-commit under one lock | Trust GET validation or update separate objects without lock | Prevents expiry/replay races and partial success; lock/store is single-process only. |
| One neutral invalid-link state | Separate public errors for used vs expired vs unknown | Minimizes token/account leakage; copy and layout are not prescribed by the wireframe. |
| Minimal nonempty password validation with hashing | Invent mandatory complexity rules | Avoids presenting unspecified policy as evidence; decide any extra local bounds for resource safety, not as a normative password rule. |
| Same `200` acknowledgement for all syntactically valid reset requests | Different status, redirect, error or flash on throttling/unknown | Makes observable status/body/headers parity testable; timing attacks are not solved by that claim. |

## Assumptions and questions carried forward

**Assumptions (not evidence):** A1 synthetic credentials may sign in to demonstrate sessions; no specific account list, password policy or signed-in content is specified. A2 account identifier is normalized email and only the sign-in page is visually specified; all reset layouts/text above are proposed. A3 known-account links and owner notifications are inspectable only inside the private process-local sink, not on public pages; there is no email delivery. A4 the five-per-hour rule applies to accepted requests for a known account over a rolling hour; no made-up quota for nonexistent accounts. A5 a link is usable strictly before, and invalid at or after, `issued_at + 30 minutes`. A6 a single Flask process is the demonstration scope; crash/restart loses state. The suggested CSRF/cookie/validation details are design choices, not statements of a further standard.

**Open questions (non-blocking for proposed local prototype):** Which exact recovery/error/success copy and minimal signed-in result should be approved? Is an additional password policy required beyond a nonempty masked input? Should all invalid/used/expired links share the neutral wording chosen here? What authorized same-process sink inspection workflow is preferred for local demonstrators? What accessible validation/progress treatment and HTTP cache/cookie defaults should reviewers approve? If production use were ever separately scoped, who owns durability, anti-enumeration timing analysis, multi-instance limits/session revocation, secret rotation, real delivery and privacy review? These are not resolved by this note.
